title: Finding flow on local trails
author: FKoko
excerpt: A short after-school ride, technical sections and a surprisingly good feeling.

content.text: There's something about the local trails that keeps pulling me back. Not because they're the most technical or the longest, but because they're where I learned to ride. Every root, every rock, every corner — I know them all.
Today was supposed to be an easy spin. Two hours, zone 2, nothing crazy. But the legs felt good and the trails were running fast after yesterday's rain. So I opened it up a bit.
The technical section

There's a rocky descent I've been working on for months. It's short, maybe 200 meters, but it's steep, loose, and has a tight left-hander at the bottom. Today I cleared it for the first time without touching the brakes.
The trail doesn't care how fast you were last time. It only cares about right now.
That's the thing about flow. You can't force it. You can't chase it. It shows up when you stop thinking and just ride. Today I stopped thinking.
Nothing groundbreaking. Just a good ride on familiar trails with a clear head. Those are the best kind.

title: FTP test and what it told me
author: FKoko
excerpt: Did my first proper FTP test in months. The number was better than expected, but the lessons were bigger.

content.text: I've been avoiding the FTP test for weeks. Not because I was scared of the number, but because I knew I hadn't been training as consistently as I should. School, work, life — the usual excuses.
But yesterday I bit the bullet. Twenty-minute warm-up, then the ramp test. And honestly? It went better than I expected.
The numbers
Three watts isn't a lot. But it's something. And it tells me the training is working, even if it doesn't feel like it day to day.
Progress is never linear. But it's always forward, even when it doesn't feel like it.
The bigger takeaway was my heart rate response. My LTHR came in at 183 bpm, which matches what I've been seeing on hard climbs. That means my zones are dialed correctly and I can trust the numbers.
Next step: build a proper polarized plan around this. More zone 2, more intensity, less junk miles.

title: New carbon wheels: first impressions
author: FKoko
excerpt: After months on alloy rims, I switched to carbon. Here's what changed and whether it was worth it.

content.text: I've been riding alloy wheels for two seasons. They were reliable, stiff enough, and I never thought about them. Which is exactly what you want from wheels.
But when a set of LightCarbon carbon rims came up at a price I couldn't ignore, I pulled the trigger. Here are my first impressions after 200km.
The weight
400 grams doesn't sound like much, but you feel it. Acceleration is snappier, especially out of corners. Climbing feels marginally easier, though that might be placebo.
Stiffness and handling
The carbon rims are noticeably stiffer laterally. In hard cornering the bike tracks straighter and feels more precise. No flex, no wandering.
Good wheels don't make you faster. They make the bike faster. You just get to come along for the ride.
Was it worth it? For racing, yes. For casual riding, absolutely not. But I'm racing, so here we are.

title: First XC race of the season
author: FKoko
excerpt: Nervous start, messy first lap, but I found my rhythm. Here's how it went down.

content.text: I lined up for my first XC race of the season on Sunday. I'd been training for it, but nothing prepares you for that start-line feeling. The heart rate spikes before you even clip in.
The start

I got a decent start — not last into the singletrack, but not first either. The first lap was chaos. Everyone fresh, everyone fighting for position, and I made the mistake of going too hard on the opening climb.
By lap two I'd settled into a rhythm. Found a group, worked with them on the climbs, and pushed on the descents where I felt comfortable.
Racing isn't about being the strongest. It's about being the strongest when it matters.
Finished 14th out of 38 in my category. Not a podium, but I'll take it. The legs were there, the handling was there, and most importantly, I didn't blow up. Progress.

title: Why I ride
author: FKoko
excerpt: Not for medals or Strava kudos. Here's what keeps me coming back to the bike.

content.text: People ask me why I ride. The honest answer changes depending on the day, the weather, and how the legs feel.
Some days it's the competition. The desire to be faster, to push harder, to see what I'm capable of. Other days it's the escape — the trails, the trees, the silence between shifts.
The bike doesn't care about your excuses. It only cares about your effort.
But mostly, I ride because it's the one thing in my life that's entirely mine. No group projects, no deadlines, no compromises. Just me, the trail, and how hard I'm willing to work.
That's why I ride. Not for medals or kudos. For the clarity.

title: Cockpit setup changes
author: FKoko
excerpt: Went wider on the bar and shorter on the stem. Here's what it changed about the handling.

content.text: I've been running a 720mm bar with a 100mm stem for two seasons. It worked, but on steep technical descents I always felt like I was fighting the bike rather than steering it.
So I went wider and shorter: 760mm carbon bar, 90mm stem. The difference was immediate.
What changed
The wider bar gives more leverage on technical sections. The shorter stem makes the steering quicker without feeling twitchy. On steep descents I have more control and more confidence.
The right cockpit doesn't make you a better rider. It removes the excuses.
On climbs, the shorter stem puts me slightly more forward, which helps on steep gradients. The trade-off is slightly less weight on the front wheel on flat corners, but I've adjusted.
Overall, this is the best setup change I've made. Small adjustment, big difference.
